<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

In mixed sync/async CPU-tier loads, submit and wait for sync jobs before the forward, then defer independent async-job submission until OffloadingConnector collects transfer results. This removes async host-side submission from the pre-forward path; it does not guarantee a lower TTFT or higher throughput.

## Claims

- Sync jobs remain submitted and awaited before the forward. Independent async jobs are staged and submitted once from OffloadingConnector's existing `get_finished()` hook.
- The change can reduce forward-start delay when async host submission would otherwise hold up the model runner. It does not make the async H2D copy overlap the current target forward.
- The size of any end-to-end benefit depends on available forward work to overlap and on how long async submission takes. If the GPU is already continuously busy, this change does not add GPU capacity; deferred submission can also delay async-load completion.

## Validation

Focused tests cover mixed sync/async loads, deferred submission through `get_finished()`, no-forward steps, and transfer completion/error handling. Ruff and pre-commit checks passed.

A timeline probe used Qwen3-4B, TP=2, and 24 concurrent requests (16 with a warmed 512-token CPU-cache prefix plus a 480-token uncached suffix; 8 uncached 992-token prompts; one output token each). Each captured mixed step had 2 sync and 14 async jobs, with 9 requests and 7904 tokens scheduled. One burst was recorded for each of four scenarios.

The `Before` panels are a controlled pre-forward-submission reference using the same instrumented code and workload. They are not measurements from a checkout of the historical PR base.

| Runner path | Before: async submission overlap with target forward | PR: async submission overlap with target forward |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| MRv1 | 0 ms | 15.47 ms |
| MRv2 | 0 ms | 17.28 ms |

### MRv1 timelines

Controlled pre-forward reference:

![MRv1 pre-forward submission reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Alex-ai-future/vllm/c9731fb8c3f56944f4d02e76c12ad51d4729da6c/benchmarks/kv_offload_overlap_figures/mr1-before.png)

This PR, using the MRv1 result-collection hook:

![MRv1 PR result hook](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Alex-ai-future/vllm/c9731fb8c3f56944f4d02e76c12ad51d4729da6c/benchmarks/kv_offload_overlap_figures/mr1-after.png)

### MRv2 timelines

Controlled pre-forward reference:

![MRv2 pre-forward submission reference](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Alex-ai-future/vllm/c9731fb8c3f56944f4d02e76c12ad51d4729da6c/benchmarks/kv_offload_overlap_figures/mr2-before.png)

This PR, using the MRv2 post-forward result-collection hook:

![MRv2 PR post-forward hook](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Alex-ai-future/vllm/c9731fb8c3f56944f4d02e76c12ad51d4729da6c/benchmarks/kv_offload_overlap_figures/mr2-after.png)

The shaded interval measures CPU-side async submission overlap, not H2D-copy overlap or GPU utilization. In these traces, the H2D copies started after target forward due to the transfer-stream dependency. This single-burst-per-scenario probe does not measure TTFT, token delivery latency, throughput, or GPU saturation, and therefore does not establish an end-to-end speedup.

## Details

[#61961](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61961) introduced sync CPU-tier hits. In a mixed step, only sync loads must complete before the current forward, but the previous submission loop also submitted independent async loads before it. This change stages those async jobs and submits them during existing result collection, without changing the shared connector interface or other connectors.

The lifecycle hook occurs at different points by runner version: MRv1 collects transfer results after forward and before sampling, so a long host submission can push sampling later if it extends past the forward's remaining GPU time. MRv2 collects results in `post_forward()` after sampling work and the token-output copy have been enqueued; host submission can still delay the runner returning its output. In both cases, async H2D completion may be later because the jobs are submitted later.

This is a follow-up to #61961 addressing mixed sync/async submission; #61961 did not split submissions by job type. AI assistance was used.

```bash
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH="$PWD" /home/jovyan/git/vllm-project/vllm/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_worker.py -k 'load_completion or mixed_loads or get_finished or no_forward_sync or failed_load or failed_sync' -q
```

- [x] I used vLLM's `/pr-checklist` skill.
- [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR.
- [x] **Design Fit:** The change is isolated to OffloadingConnector and its worker; it reuses existing lifecycle hooks.
- [x] **Testing and Validation:** Focused tests and a serving timeline probe are documented. No TTFT/throughput improvement is claimed.
- [x] **Code Quality and Style:** The shared connector interface and unrelated connectors are unchanged.
- [x] **Pull Request Contents:** The root cause, intended benefit, evidence, limitations, and relation to #61961 are documented.
</details>

Thanks @kfirtoledo I tried an end-to-end comparison with sync_load_budget_bytes set, using the same workload on the PR base and head with mixed step. It seems the TTFT can be lower in most test cases. However, the scheduler assigned requests to sync and async loads differently between runs, and queue-time variability made the results difficult to interpret. 

Do you have some better solutions?

I added end-to-end inference timeline measurements to the PR description using a mixed-load Qwen3-4B workload (TP=2, 24 concurrent requests). In the captured mixed step, both runner paths had 2 sync and 14 async load jobs.

With the new scheduling, CPU-side async submission overlapped the GPU target forward by 15.47 ms in MRv1 and 17.28 ms in MRv2; the controlled pre-forward references had no such overlap. This shows that the async submission work can use CPU time while the GPU is executing forward, keeping that work off the pre-forward path.

The H2D copies themselves remained ordered after the target forward in these traces. This measurement demonstrates host-side submission overlap; it does not claim an H2D/forward overlap or a TTFT/end-to-end latency improvement.

The graph is in the PR discription.

LGTM, thanks. Keeping async submission off the sync path makes sense, and it matches how steps without sync loads already work.

The gain is small at typical batch sizes (under 1 ms up to 16 async jobs, per your table), but I think it would be good to run a quick end-to-end test with `sync_load_budget_bytes` set to confirm queue time and TTFT don't change.
